title: Investigating how a natural hormone called kisspeptin affects social and emotional brain processing
official: Kisspeptin and the Mind: investigating the effects of kisspeptin in socio-emotional brain processing in neurotypical and neurodivergent men
summary:
Background and study aims
Autism can affect how people talk, make friends, and understand feelings and their senses. Many autistic people also feel more anxious and low, especially in social situations. Because of this, we want to learn more about how the brain controls social behaviour and emotions.

Kisspeptin is a natural hormone in the body. It is best known for helping control reproductive hormones, but research shows it can also affect how the brain works. Research from our group has shown it can change how people process certain emotions but its effects in autistic people have not yet been studied.

This study will explore how kisspeptin affects brain activity linked to social and emotional processing in autistic and non-autistic men. By comparing both groups, we hope to better understand how the brain helps people manage emotions.
 
Who can participate?
We are looking for men aged 18 to 60 years. They must be right-handed and either not autistic or have an autism diagnosis. People who are interested individuals will be invited for a first (screening) visit to check if they can take part.

Screening visit
At this visit, you will meet the research team in person. They will ask about your health and medical history and do simple checks, like measuring your blood pressure. You will also fill in some questionnaires about mood, anxiety, and thinking skills. These help the team understand how you feel and think. If you are autistic and have not already had a detailed test, the team may do one to confirm your diagnosis.

What does the study involve?
You will attend two study visits. Each visit will last about 3 hours.

At each visit:
-	You will get a small injection under the skin. This will be either kisspeptin (a natural hormone) or a placebo (salt water). You will have both, but on different days and you will not know which order you receive them. 
-	You will have a brain scan (called an fMRI). This scan shows which parts of your brain are active. 
-	During the scan, you will do simple tasks to look at how you think about emotions and social situations. 
-	Blood samples will be taken to measure hormone levels. 
-	You will fill in questionnaires about your mood and anxiety before and after the scan. 
-	At the end, you will do a short attention test.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
You will not get direct medical benefits from taking part. However, the study will help scientists learn more about how hormones affect the brain, especially in social and emotional situations. This could help future research support autistic people. 

Kisspeptin is a natural hormone and has been safely used in many studies before. Doctors and researchers will be there at all times, and you will be carefully monitored.

Where is the study run from?
The first visit will take place at Charing Cross Hospital, Imperial College London. 
The two study visits will take place at the Perceptive Clinical Imaging Centre at Hammersmith Hospital (White City, London, UK).

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
April 2026 to March 2028.

Who is funding the study?
National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) (UK).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Men aged 18–60 years
2. IQ of >70 as measured by Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence test, Second edition (WASI–II)
3. For the neurodivergent group, participants will be included only if they have received a formal Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) diagnosis from the NHS or an NHS-recognised provider
4. For the neurotypical group, we will include only participants without a prior diagnosis of ASD and who score <26 on the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) at screening
5. Right–hand dominant
6. Participants must be able to provide full informed consent. We will make every reasonable effort to accommodate a participant who does not speak English as their first language, such as using an interpreter. However, where there is doubt as to whether the potential participant can fully understand the study, we will not be able to include them as their consent would not be fully informed and there may be difficulty in performing the tasks required for the study which would impact the data collected and hence the robustness of the study
Exclusion criteria:
1. History of any medical, psychological, or other condition, or use of any medications, including over-the-counter products, which, in the opinion of the investigators, would either interfere with the study or potentially cause harm to the participant
2. Medical or psychological conditions that would impair their ability to participate reliably in the study or give informed consent
3. Any implanted material in the body that would preclude MRI for safety reasons
4. Inability to tolerate MRI scanning (e.g., claustrophobia or inability to lie flat)
5. Impaired vision which would preclude the ability to view the video material used in the study
6. Without access at home to a telephone, or other factor likely to interfere with ability to participate reliably in the study
7. History of hypersensitivity to any of the components administered
8. Participation in any research study within the preceding 30 days (or 2 months if an investigational drug was administered)
9. Those who have haemoglobin levels outside the normal reference range
